stem: A media retailer's inventory team is designing an out-of-stock alert: it must route only 'out-of-stock' events to a Lambda function, and it must pick up events that AWS services already emit automatically with no extra setup on the producing side. Which TWO EventBridge facts does this design rely on? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: An SQS standard queue can match events against a pattern the same way an EventBridge rule does
An EventBridge rule can deliver only events matching an 'out-of-stock' pattern to a Lambda target
A custom event bus must be created before any AWS service event becomes visible to the account
Every AWS account has a default event bus that automatically receives events emitted by AWS services
A Lambda function must poll the inventory table on a fixed schedule to detect the out-of-stock condition

rationale: An EventBridge rule matches incoming events against a pattern and delivers only the matches to a target, which is how only the 'out-of-stock' events reach the alert Lambda function, and every account already has a default event bus that receives AWS service events automatically, which is why no extra setup is needed on the producing side. An SQS standard queue has no pattern-matching capability at all; it delivers whatever is sent to it in order received, so it cannot filter by event content the way a rule does. A custom event bus is not required to see AWS service events, since the default bus already receives them. Polling the inventory table on a schedule is exactly the delay-and-waste pattern an event-driven design avoids; it is not part of this EventBridge-based design.
